summary: Specifies routing extensions to carry link state information for GMPLS. It enhances the routing extensions needed for MPLS Traffic Engineering. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Routers need maps of the roads available, including fancy optical ones. This memo describes what extra details those maps should hold.

questions: what is an interface switching capability descriptor
subtitle: What extra link details routers must advertise so paths can be computed over optical and TDM links, not just packet links.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering assumes a TE link is an add-on to an ordinary packet link with a routing adjacency, but GMPLS networks include optical and time-division links that cannot carry routing packets and need richer descriptions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC generalizes the TE link and adds link properties to advertise: unnumbered link identifiers, a Link Protection Type, Shared Risk Link Group information and an Interface Switching Capability Descriptor.
tldr.outcome: It defines what information is carried. How it is encoded in OSPF and IS-IS is left to companion documents, and the RFC has since been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074.

facts.label: Unnumbered link identifier
facts.value: Non-zero 32-bit number, unique within the LSR

facts.label: SRLG identifier
facts.value: 32-bit number, unique within an IGP domain

facts.label: Default switching capability
facts.value: PSC-1 when no descriptor is present

facts.label: Switching capabilities
facts.value: 8 (PSC-1 to PSC-4, L2SC, TDM, LSC, FSC)

today: RFC 4202 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6001, RFC 6002 and RFC 7074. It has not been obsoleted, according to the metadata for this RFC.

sections.title: The Generalized TE Link
sections.content:
This RFC specifies routing extensions for carrying link state information for Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS). It builds on the routing extensions for MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) in RFC 3630 (OSPF) and RFC 3784 (IS-IS).

Traditionally a TE link is an adjunct to a regular link: a routing adjacency is up on it, and its TE properties are advertised alongside. GMPLS breaks this in three ways. Links that cannot send and receive packet by packet may still have TE properties, but no routing adjacency can be brought up on them. A Label Switched Path can be advertised as a point-to-point TE link between nodes with no adjacency. And several links may be advertised as one TE link.

So a TE link is now a logical link with TE properties, a way to group information about physical resources into what constrained shortest path first (CSPF) computation and GMPLS signaling use. Both ends must do the grouping consistently, and the Link Management Protocol (RFC 4204) can verify that. The advertising router needs some means of knowing the link is alive, which may be routing hellos but need not be. The interfaces carrying regular routing adjacencies are called control channels.
sections.eli5: A road on the map used to always be a road you could drive on. Now some roads are really pipes of light, so the map needs a bigger idea of what a road is.

sections.title: Layer-Specific Requirements
sections.content:
Transport networks add needs that packet networks lack. Clients may need a connection at a specific adaptation, for example a VC-3 circuit of 48.384 Mbit/s with the expected structure, not just some amount of bandwidth. One resource can support several adaptations at once, which creates dependencies between layers. Attributes can be inherited: an OC-192 link that is 1+1 protected passes that protection to an STS-3c inside it. New layers may appear later, and in a heterogeneous network not every switch supports the same layers.

From this the RFC gives principles for layer-specific TE attributes: separate attributes per layer, support for inter-layer relationships, support for inheritable attributes, layer extensibility, and explicit attribute scope.

This document only captures general attributes of a single layer network. Inter-layer relationships are left to a future document.
sections.eli5: Different kinds of pipes carry things in different-sized pieces, and a trip needs the right-sized piece. The map has to say what each pipe can really carry.

sections.title: Keeping Data Off Control Channels
sections.content:
Control channels carry control and administrative traffic such as RSVP messages. They are advertised into routing as normal links, so edge routers might try to send user data over them and quickly exhaust their capacity.

One technique restricts BGP next-hop resolution. When router R installs a route to a BGP destination D, it finds the interface I toward the next hop. If R has a link state database entry for I and that link is not packet-switch capable, R installs a discard route for D. Otherwise it installs the usual route via I. The RFC assumes OXCs are not BGP speakers, and R only needs the check if it has packet-switch incapable links.

In another approach, a carrier keeps the address space of its GMPLS routing plane separate from the data endpoints and never advertises control channels into the data network. The RFC adds that other techniques may also be needed.
sections.eli5: The little service road for workers must not fill up with regular traffic. Routers are told not to send everyday cars down it.

sections.title: Unnumbered Links, Protection and Risk Groups
sections.content:
An unnumbered link must be point-to-point. The LSR at each end assigns it an identifier, a non-zero 32-bit number unique within that LSR. An advertisement carries both the local and the remote identifier. If the LSR does not know the remote identifier, it should use 0.

The Link Protection Type says what protection exists for a link, so path computation can find paths meeting a minimum protection level. The RFC lists them from lowest to highest: Extra Traffic, Unprotected, Shared, Dedicated 1:1, Dedicated 1+1 and Enhanced. It is optional, and if absent the protection type is unknown.

A set of links is a shared risk link group (SRLG) if they share a resource whose failure may affect all of them, like two fibers in one conduit. An SRLG is identified by a 32-bit number unique within an IGP domain, and a link can be in several. When diverse paths are needed, path computation should try to make the paths link-disjoint and their SRLGs disjoint. SRLG information is also optional, and if absent the SRLG of the link is unknown.
sections.eli5: Each end of a pipe can give it its own nickname. The map also notes how well each pipe is backed up, and which pipes share a trench, so one digging accident does not cut both of your routes.

sections.title: Interface Switching Capability Descriptor
sections.content:
An interface connects a link to a node, and it may not switch individual packets. The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor describes what an interface can switch. Its capabilities are defined as the same in both directions, a link advertisement carries only the near-end descriptors, and the two ends of a bidirectional link may differ. The defined capabilities are PSC-1 to PSC-4, L2SC, TDM, LSC and FSC. If no descriptor is present, the interface is assumed to be PSC-1. The descriptor always carries the encoding the interface supports.

The extra data depends on the type. PSC interfaces add Maximum LSP Bandwidth, Minimum LSP Bandwidth and interface MTU. Maximum LSP Bandwidth is carried per priority and replaces the single fixed Maximum Link Bandwidth. TDM interfaces add Maximum and Minimum LSP Bandwidth and whether Standard or Arbitrary SDH is supported. LSC interfaces add Reservable Bandwidth per priority. FSC interfaces switch the entire interface contents and cannot restrict themselves to one lambda.

An interface can have more than one descriptor, for multiple capabilities, for bandwidth that differs by priority, or for discrete bandwidths. The descriptor can also change over time as LSPs are set up. The meaning of a label depends on the capabilities at both ends of the link, as shown in the table.
sections.eli5: Each doorway into a building has a sign: this door takes single letters, that one takes whole sacks, another takes whole trucks. The sign tells planners which doors fit their load.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives descriptors for real device types. A STM-16 POS interface on an LSR is PSC-1 with SDH encoding and a Max LSP Bandwidth of 2.5 Gbps for all priorities. A GigE packet interface is PSC-1 with Ethernet 802.3 encoding and 1.0 Gbps. An STM-64 interface on a digital cross connect with Standard SDH is TDM with a Min LSP Bandwidth of VC-3 and a Max of STM-64.

For optical devices, an interface on an opaque OXC handles one wavelength and is always LSC, never FSC. A transparent OXC (PXC) with an external DWDM that limits a port to one wavelength is also LSC. With no external DWDM between two PXCs, the interface is advertised as FSC. Devices combining functions, such as PXC+TDM or TDM+LSR, are treated as one interface described by two descriptors, for example one LSC and one TDM.
sections.eli5: The memo fills in the signs for a bunch of real machines, so you can see how a fiber switch gets a different sign than a regular router.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that there are a number of security concerns, particularly because these extensions will potentially be used to control the underlying transport infrastructure. It is vital to have secure or authenticated means of transferring this information among the entities that need it.

This document does not say how the extensions are carried in OSPF or IS-IS. The documents that do, RFC 4203 and RFC 4205, must also state how the information is secured.
sections.eli5: If someone could change the map, they could send traffic the wrong way, so the map must only be shared with trusted friends.

viz.caption: LINK PROTECTION TYPES, LOWEST TO HIGHEST PROTECTION (RFC 4202)

items.label: Extra Traffic
items.desc: Link protects other links; its LSPs are lost if a protected link fails.

items.label: Unprotected
items.desc: No other link protects this link.

items.label: Shared
items.desc: One or more disjoint Extra Traffic links protect it and are shared.

items.label: Dedicated 1:1
items.desc: One dedicated disjoint Extra Traffic link protects it.

items.label: Dedicated 1+1
items.desc: A dedicated link protects it but is not advertised for routing LSPs.

items.label: Enhanced
items.desc: A scheme more reliable than Dedicated 1+1, e.g. 4 fiber BLSR/MS-SPRING.
